recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This is a detailed image of NGC 6240, a galaxy in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, taken with the Dark Energy Camera, or DECam.

The US Department of Energy built DECam, and it sits on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile, part of NSF NOIRLab. It is a wide-field camera, designed to photograph large areas of sky in a single exposure while still picking up faint objects.

For NGC 6240 it recorded light through three filters, known as g, r and z. The g and r filters cover parts of the visible spectrum, while z reaches into near-infrared light just beyond what human eyes can see. Combining separate exposures like these is how astronomers build a color image. Each filter is assigned a color, and together they approximate the full picture. Observing across several wavelengths also helps astronomers compare how different kinds of stars, gas and dust contribute to a galaxy's light.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 6240 through g, r and z filters, covering visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
